newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis completes four months, no sign of end.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis completes four months, no sign of end.

text.p: The Lima hostage crisis ended its fourth month on Wednesday with no public sign the 72 captives would be freed any time soon despite frenetic behind-the-scenes activity by key players in the drama.

A hectic schedule of separate meetings between members of a guarantors' commission and negotiators for both the Peruvian government and the Marxist rebels in recent days has kept Peruvians speculating about a possible solution.

But the government and rebels have not met face-to-face since March 12. All sides have held to a strict code of silence about the contents of their discussions and outside observers are divided in their interpretation of events.
Some say a negotiated solution could be announced at any time, while others argue the lengthy meetings indicate just how much still separates the two sides.
"It's idle to bet either way. At this stage it's just impossible to say when this could end," one Western diplomat said. "No one would ever have imagined it going on this long in the first place."
The main sticking point in the 120-day crisis remains the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels' demand for the release of jailed comrades.

In one of the few public notes of optimism, Peru's ambassador in Bolivia, Harry Belevan, said the crisis "was on track towards its final stage." But, in comments reported by local media, he did not elaborate.

While the MRTA's Dec. 17 takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima astounded the world and dominated headlines in its early weeks, interest in the fate of the hostages has now waned dramatically.

Even in Peru, none of the major local newspapers mentioned the crisis on Wednesday on its front page. Instead, they concentrated on the growing scandal surrounding the torture of an army intelligence officer and the murder of another and on negotiations with Ecuador over a border dispute.

But in a reminder of the underlying tension around the crisis, the government extended for another two months the state of emergency it enforced in December around the besieged residence in the upscale San Isidro district. It also extended the state of emergency for 60 days in 12 mainly outlying poor districts of Lima that are traditional hotbeds of leftist guerrilla activity.
Despite a dramatic drop in violence since the peak of the guerrilla warfare between the mid-1980s and the early 1990s, about 30 percent of Peru is still under a state of emergency.

Police believe MRTA members have been approaching the diplomatic residence disguised as street vendors or journalists to do intelligence work and contact comrades inside. Various suspects have been arrested by anti-terrorism police using emergency laws.
